# Takkalajātaka (Ja 446)

**ID:** Ja 446
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Takkalajātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul9.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Takkalajātaka* (Ja 446) is a canonical Jātaka tale belonging to the Khuddaka Nikāya. According to the traditional framing narrative, the Buddha delivered this discourse while residing at Jetavana regarding a dutiful layman who supported his father.

In the verse narrative preserved in the commentary, a young boy confronts his father as the latter begins digging a square pit in the midst of a cemetery in the forest, asking why he is digging a hole when there are no edible bulbs (*takkalā*), tubers (*ālupāni*), or roots to be found (*na takkaḷā santi na ālupāni...*) [Fausböll 1887]. The aṭṭhakathā explains *takkalā* as a type of bulbous root (*piṇḍālukanda*) [Fausböll 1887]. At the conclusion of the story's teaching of the truths, the devoted son who maintained his father attains the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*), and the Buddha identifies himself as having been the wise boy (*paṇḍitakumāra*) in that past life [Fausböll 1887].

**Sources**

- [Fausböll 1887] V. Fausböll, Jātaka together with its Commentary, Vol. 4 (1887) — Pali verses, commentarial definitions of roots, and the narrative conclusion including the samodhāna and attainment of stream-entry.
